opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important shifts in the whole field right now, and in some ways it's a return to first principles.

If you look at the last few years, the main paradigm was pretraining plus a bit of alignment. You scale up data, scale up compute, and the model gets smarter by predicting the next token. That worked incredibly well. But there's a natural ceiling: high-quality human-generated data is finite. At some point you're no longer limited by compute but by the data itself. So the question becomes: where does the next increment of intelligence come from?

Reinforcement learning is a very natural answer, because it lets the model generate its own data. It tries something, gets feedback from the environment, a verifier, or a reward signal, and improves from that. You're turning compute into data, and that changes the scaling picture quite fundamentally. Long chain-of-thought reasoning is one example. The model learns to think longer, reflect, backtrack, and correct itself, and these behaviors largely emerge from RL rather than being hand-designed.

The shift from dialogue to agents is closely connected. A chat model is basically one-turn or few-turn: you ask, it answers, and the human is still doing most of the work of deciding what to do next. An agent can take a task, break it down, call tools, browse, write and run code, observe the results, and keep going over many steps until the task is done. That's a much bigger lever on productivity. The value isn't just in giving a good answer but in actually completing work.

And you can't really get good agents purely from imitation, because there's very little human data for long-horizon, multi-step tool use. You need the model to interact with environments and learn from outcomes, which is again reinforcement learning. So I see the two as the same trend: the model moves from a passive predictor to an active learner and doer.

For a company like ours, this also changes how you organize R&D. Before, a lot of the effort went into data pipelines and pretraining infrastructure. Now you also need to build environments, design good reward signals, and handle RL infrastructure, which is quite hard to make stable and efficient at scale. Taste matters a lot too: choosing which tasks and which feedback signals actually lead to generalizable capability, rather than overfitting to a benchmark.

So I'd say it's not a minor adjustment. Pretraining gives the model its base of knowledge, but RL and agentic training are what turn that knowledge into the ability to reason and act. I think that's where a big part of the next phase of progress toward AGI will come from.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift changes how the company organizes R&D, describing a move from data pipelines and pretraining infrastructure toward building environments, reward signals, and RL infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this shift is fundamental, not incremental. For the past few years the industry has essentially been running one paradigm: next-token prediction on static data. That paradigm is extremely good at compressing human knowledge, but it has a ceiling, and that ceiling is the data itself. We're approaching the point where high-quality human text is largely consumed. So the question becomes: where does the next order-of-magnitude improvement come from?

My answer is that it comes from the model generating its own experience. Reinforcement learning is the mechanism for that. Instead of only learning from what humans have already written, the model acts, gets feedback from an environment, and improves on signals that no one hand-labeled. That's a qualitatively different source of intelligence. Pretraining gives you the prior; RL is how you convert that prior into real capability on long-horizon tasks.

This is also why I see the move from dialogue to agents as a natural consequence rather than a separate trend. A chat product is fundamentally one turn in, one turn out. The value is bounded by how much a human can read and verify in a sitting. An agent breaks that constraint. It can run for hours, call tools, check its own work, and come back with a result. Once you measure value in completed tasks rather than in pleasant answers, the economics change completely, and the kind of training you need changes with it. You can't get reliable long-horizon behavior from imitation alone, because errors compound. You need the model to be optimized against outcomes.

From an R&D organization standpoint, this means a lot of things shift. Data teams become environment and reward teams. Evaluation stops being "does this response look good" and becomes "did this task actually get done." Infrastructure has to support massive amounts of rollout, which is a different engineering problem from scaling pretraining. And product has to be designed around trust and verification, because you're delegating more.

I'd also say there's a strategic dimension. In pretraining, scale is largely a function of capital, and frankly the frontier labs with the most compute have a structural advantage. In RL, the bottleneck is more about problem design, environments, and the ability to iterate quickly on what to reward. That rewards taste and focus, not just budget. For a team like ours, that's an opening.

The risk, of course, is reward hacking and brittleness. If the signal is wrong, RL will find the loophole faster than any human would. So a lot of the hard work is not in the algorithm but in building verifiable tasks and keeping the model honest. But I think that's the right problem to be working on. The last era was about teaching models what people know. This era is about teaching them to do things. I don't think there's a more important direction right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift to agents changes the R&D organization’s work, including turning data teams toward environments and rewards, changing evaluation, and requiring different infrastructure and product design.

astra-6.text:
I think these two shifts are closely connected. Moving from dialogue to agents changes what we ask a model to do. It needs to take actions, observe the results, adjust its approach, and keep working toward a goal. That makes the ability to learn from outcomes increasingly important.

Reinforcement learning is a natural way to develop that ability. But the challenge goes beyond choosing an algorithm. You need environments where the model can practice meaningful tasks, reliable feedback on whether it succeeded, and a training process that turns that feedback into capabilities that generalize. If the reward is easy to measure but doesn’t reflect what users actually want, you can optimize it without making the agent more useful.

So I see this as a shift in the whole R&D process. Pretraining still provides the foundation, while more of the work becomes about building a loop between learning, acting, and evaluating results. The important test is whether the model can reliably complete increasingly complex tasks with less human intervention. That’s where the move toward agents becomes meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift to agents changes the whole R&D process, describing a move toward learning, acting, and evaluating results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think these two shifts are closely connected. Moving from dialogue to agents changes what we want a model to do: instead of just producing a good answer, it needs to take actions, observe the results, and keep working toward a goal. That puts much more emphasis on learning from outcomes.

Supervised learning can teach a model to imitate a useful response or a successful trajectory. But for an agent, there are many possible paths, and you can’t write demonstrations for every situation. Reinforcement learning gives us a way to improve through exploration and feedback, including when the reward comes only after a long sequence of actions.

So the R&D challenge becomes broader than designing a training algorithm. You need environments where the model can act, tasks with meaningful feedback, and evaluations that tell you whether it actually completed the work. You also need to make that whole process efficient enough to iterate.

I wouldn’t describe this as abandoning dialogue or pretraining. They remain foundations. But the emphasis moves toward whether the model can reliably accomplish something. That’s why I see agents as an important direction for the product, and reinforcement learning as an important direction for the research supporting it.

r001.rationale: The response says the shift broadens the R&D work to include building action environments, meaningful feedback, evaluations, and efficient iteration, clearly describing a substantial change in how the team works.
